rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs. The strong endpoint reduces truncation risk, while a moderate temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.
Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to probe selectivity changes in the central cluster and late doublet. This isolates temperature effects while preserving a short, nontruncated run.

Use a shallower gradient at the better-performing temperature to test whether the remaining close pairs gain resolution. The current short elution window leaves substantial room to spread peaks before incurring a time penalty.

The shallower gradient resolved the central cluster but created one close pair near 6.7 minutes. Lower temperature by one grid step to shift that pair’s selectivity while retaining the improved gradient separation and time margin.

Test the shallow gradient at 40 °C to seek separation on the opposite side of the temperature-sensitive central co-elution. Comparing this with injection 1 also reveals how strongly gradient slope changes selectivity at this temperature.

Shorten the 40 °C gradient to move the close pair near 7.4 minutes away from its shallow-gradient co-elution. This also creates time margin, while testing whether the other resolved pairs retain sufficient separation.

At 60 °C, shorten the shallow gradient to move away from the near-co-elution seen at 24 minutes. This tests whether the late pair can separate while the central cluster retains the resolution gained with a shallower gradient.

This gradient is about 5% steeper than injection 7, targeting improved separation of the remaining critical pair while preserving the central cluster’s small resolution margin. Adjusting both endpoint and duration provides a finer slope change than shortening tG alone.

Increase the slope slightly from 0.04444 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute, aiming to lift the remaining R = 1.49 pair above 1.5 without losing central-cluster resolution. All peaks should elute before this gradient ends, so the lower endpoint should not affect their elution.

Injection 9 achieved the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark. Test a slightly steeper slope of 0.04583 per minute to seek earlier elution while checking whether the central pairs remain above R = 1.5.

The steeper-slope test crossed the resolution boundary, so retain injection 9 as the maximum-score benchmark. Raise the starting organic fraction while reducing slope to test whether a narrower gradient window can shorten elution without sacrificing full resolution.

Reduce the slope at the higher starting organic fraction to recover resolution of the early critical pair. This tests whether full resolution can be restored while retaining some of injection 11’s time advantage; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

The higher starting organic fraction produced competing resolution losses, so test a lower start with a steeper gradient instead. This may improve the early critical pair enough to permit faster separation; injection 9 remains the proven maximum-score method.

Injection 9 already achieves the maximum score, but nearby high-temperature methods show little room for shortening. Test a lower-temperature selectivity regime with a steeper gradient to seek another fully resolved, short method.

Shorten the low-temperature gradient to test whether slope changes separate the close central pair while bringing the last peak earlier. Injection 9 remains the fully resolved, maximum-score benchmark.

Raise temperature one step at the faster low-temperature gradient to test whether selectivity improves the two unresolved pairs. This preserves the short elution window while injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction shifts the remaining central co-elution at 30 °C while shortening retention. Injection 9 remains the proven maximum-score method, so this run explores a potentially faster alternative.

Steepen the gradient at 30 °C to move the central pair farther from its apparent slope-dependent crossing and shorten the run. The other pairs in injection 17 have useful resolution margins, though their separation will need checking.

Lower temperature one step while keeping injection 18’s fast gradient fixed to test whether the two central pairs improve together. Watch the late pair for a competing loss of resolution; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a slope close to injection 17’s to shift central-pair selectivity and shorten retention. This explores a faster alternative while retaining injection 9 as the proven maximum-score method.

Lower temperature one step to improve the remaining central pair, following the favorable central-cluster response seen in injections 18–19. Check whether the late pair retains full resolution at this higher starting organic fraction.

Make injection 21’s gradient slightly shallower to lift the late pair from R = 1.43 toward full resolution. The central pair’s R = 1.62 provides a small margin for this adjustment, potentially yielding a maximum-score method much faster than injection 9.

Injection 22 matches the maximum CRF with much earlier elution. Raise the starting organic fraction one step, slightly reducing slope, to seek further time savings while checking the two pairs closest to the resolution threshold.

Reduce the slope slightly to recover the R = 1.41 central pair while maintaining the higher starting organic fraction’s time advantage. The other pairs have resolution margin, making this a promising route to full resolution in less time than injection 22.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower slope to seek further time savings while compensating for the central pair’s loss of resolution as phi0 rises. Retain injection 24 as the fastest proven fully resolved method if this final adjustment falls short.
